extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, law, and French literature (readers of Montesquieu and annotated editions)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial/critical notes on Montesquieu's L'Esprit des lois (annotations, definitions, historical and normative commentary). The page gives explanatory definitions, historical corrections, and normative judgments about political institutions, law, education, and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align education with social condition
rubrics_metrics.description: «aujourd'hui on s'efforce davantage de mettre l'éducation en harmonie avec l'état social dans lequel nous sommes.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should be adapted to the present social condition rather than remain unrelated to the world young people will enter; editorial observation advocating practical alignment of education and social realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of honour as beauty not goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C59: «Non comme bonnes, mais comme belles.» — the true principle of honour is that actions appear beautiful and honourable (not necessarily 'good').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honour is socially perceived beauty of action within a condition; different actions appear honourable in different social positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle on slavery and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C61: Aristotle's alternative: if slaves have virtues, how differ from free men; if denied, absurd because they are men — Aristotle adds 'Le maître est l'origine de la vertu de son esclave.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to frame the problem of slavery and moral agency; citation shows tension in attributing virtue to slaves and locates origin of slave virtue in the master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid romanticizing ancient heroism
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C62: «Nos petites âmes.» — don't exaggerate antiquity's heroism; French history has comparable heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial corrective: distance illusions of ancient superiority by citing comparable national examples (e.g., Du Guesclin, Bayard, Jeanne d'Arc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of education in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C63: «C'est en vertu de la même loi que la France, depuis qu'elle est en république, a donné le pas sur tous les autres problèmes politiques aux questions d'éducation.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republics place education among top political concerns; public administration (minister of public instruction) becomes primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize fictional references
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C64: Identification of 'Sévarambes' as a fictional people (Vairasse d'Alais).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a political text cites imaginary peoples, annotate to identify sources and genre (political novel) for correct interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess customary practices by circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C65: On Sparta's permitted larceny — Rollin explains context: done at marked time, by command, limited to food, intended to teach vigilance, hardiness, frugality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate controversial institutions by weighing circumstances and motives rather than immediate moral condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat obscure ancient sources cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C66: Information on Lycurgus is very obscure; earliest sources (Herodotus) postdate Lycurgus by centuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical claims about ancient lawgivers require caution and awareness of source limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false analogies between dissimilar figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C67: Comparing William Penn to Lycurgus is arbitrary since Quakers abhor war; Voltaire rightly objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate leaders with incompatible principles (e.g., pacifist colonists vs. Spartan legislator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-of-goods limited to rudimentary societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C69: Montesquieu's proposals (community of goods, proscription of money, separation from foreigners, monopolies under magistrate) are applicable only to rudimentary societies and are contrary to liberty and civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such institutions may have historical existence but are unsuitable and dangerous in advanced/civilized societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption is not sole cause for abandoning ancient institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C70: Montesquieu attributes abandonment of practices to corruption; editor argues that's mistaken and links such ideas to Jacobin doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of attributing institutional change only to moral decline; consider structural and contextual factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and gymnastics both form the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C71: Following Plato, music and gymnastics both shape the soul differently: poetry/ harmony soften and civilize courage; gymnastics give sense of strength and energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational curricula in republics should balance culture (music/poetry) and physical training to form complementary civic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical modes have political-moral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C72: Plato's analysis of modes (phrygian, dorian energetic; ionian, lydian 'lax') indicates certain modes suit warlike character and others festal softness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural elements (music) are interpreted as influencing civic temperament; cite classical authorities when discussing moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law and government principle interact (action/reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C73: «le principe du gouvernement exerce une action sur les lois du législateur, et que ces lois à leur tour exercent leur action sur le principe du gouvernement» — analogy to mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize mutual causation between constitutional principle and enacted laws; laws both express and reshape the governmental principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue defined as public attachment to the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C74: 'La vertu dans une république' = love of the State and the form of government (public virtue), not merely private virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing civic virtue, focus on attachment to public institutions and the republic's form; question if similar attachment exists under monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican frugality as a contested ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes C75–C78: Montesquieu links frugality and limitation of pleasures to republics; editor disputes this and criticizes laws enforcing frugality as contrary to individual rights and modern democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between historical republican ideals (frugality, sumptuary laws) and modern democratic values (individual rights, equality of opportunity); avoid legislating private satisfactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question historical attributions (Lycurgus land partition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C79: Fustel de Coulanges shows it's a historical error to say Lycurgus instituted land partition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct historical assertions using up-to-date scholarship; annotate dubious classical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law should not micromanage property transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C80: Montesquieu's prescription that law should regulate dowries, donations, wills, etc., is criticized as contrary to property rights, freedom of work and exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern legal principles favor protecting property and freedom of contract over pervasive legal restriction of personal transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient laws not universally necessary today
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C81: Laws fitting ancient institutions need not apply to modern democracies; they may be wrong or unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate statutes in their historical institutional context before applying them to modern systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phaleas/Aristotle on equality of fortune criticized
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C83: Aristotle refutes Phaleas' proposals: mere equal distribution of land does not equalize fortune; must consider slaves, herds, money; revolution can stem from inequality of men as well as fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals for equalizing property must address all elements of wealth and social structure; simplistic land division is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality acceptable if natural, not legally privileged
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C84: 'L'inégalité résultant du libre emploi des facultés individuelles... n'a rien de contraire à l'égalité' — democracy condemns unequal legal privileges, not natural differences of merit/function/property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between lawful equal opportunity and unlawful legal privileges; democratic meritocracy tolerates natural inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law should secure property freedom, not enforce small shares
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C85: The law should ensure freedom of property/exchange; it need not and should not directly make shares 'small'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using legal coercion to engineer particular distributions of private wealth beyond protecting equal rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commerce can reconcile wealth with republican virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C86: In commercial states, wealth and industry may coexist with republican virtues; but education and civic virtue are better remedies than restrictive laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic development (commerce) changes social dispositions; protective legal constraints are less effective than civic education in preventing corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolish state monopolies and open access
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C87: 'Le fassent eux-mêmes' — destroy monopolies, especially state-held ones; question privileging 'principal citizens' only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate broad participation in economic opportunities rather than preserving exclusive privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal partition in succession as democratic foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C89: The law of equal share among children in inheritance is fundamental to civil law democracy; though a 'quotité disponible' remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal inheritance rules support democratic equality; degree of discretionary share varies with democratic intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware state-imposed guarantee of necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C90: 'Chacun doit l'avoir.' — If the State obliges every citizen to have necessities it commits to provide means, implying a 'right to work' and expansive state provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify implications of asserting rights to necessities; legal obligations to provide can create large state responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate life tenure questionable for democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes C92–C94: Senators 'choisis pour la vie' may be aristocratic rather than democratic; appointment for life better suits ancient small republics than modern states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional designs (life tenure vs rotation) for compatibility with democratic principles and practical functions (tradition vs preparing affairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance tradition and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C93: Societies rely on customs and institutions but human perfectibility implies change; legislatures/senates must find the balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should weigh persistence of customs against need for reform; role of upper chamber is to modulate progress and preserve continuity without blocking necessary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of civil and military in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C126: 'Les emplois civils et militaires. Il faut les unir dans les républiques.' Editor contends the opposite: modern democracies require separation to avoid military domination or absorption by civil power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain civil-military separation where standing armies are necessary to preserve liberty and effective defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure institution archaic; press as modern censor
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C129: 'Il faut des censeurs dans une république.' — editor says ancient censor institutions are incompatible with modern states; the press plays the censoring role though it too may need checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer free press for moral policing of moeurs; consider safeguards against press excesses rather than reinstating formal censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn sale of justice and vénalité of offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C128: Selling justice ('vénalité des charges judiciaires') was criticized; abolition during the Revolution; confusion between sale of judicial charges and other offices noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling judicial office undermines justice; legal and fiscal reforms should distinguish and correct vénalité practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of legal terms (Substitutions, Retrait lignager, Cession de biens, Acquêts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes C105–C106, C118, C121: Substitutions = appointing successive heirs so first cannot alienate property; Retrait lignager = right to reclaim sold inheritance by restituting price (family/right of lineage); Cession de biens = debtor frees himself by abandoning possessions; Acquêts = property acquired during marriage (community property) vs propres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise jurisprudential definitions for readers; these legal terms inform interpretation of Montesquieu's references to inheritance and property law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Péculat (concussion) as feature of despotic administrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C119: 'Le péculat est naturel dans les États despotiques.' — péculat = administrator paying himself from public funds; editor treats Montesquieu's phrase as factual condemnation of despotic systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the concept to criticize despotic governments where administrative embezzlement is systemic; modern societies abolish such practices (confiscations) as progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of confiscation as modern progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C120: 'Les confiscations... C'est l'honneur de la société moderne d'avoir aboli le principe de la confiscation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight legal reforms that end confiscatory penalties as markers of civilized legal progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion can both augment despot's power and temper it
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C112: In the Ottoman case, the sultan's role as head of religion is 'une crainte ajoutée à de la crainte' but also a limit since the mufti advises on capital punishment; contrast with Persia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the institutional interaction of religious authority and political power: religion may reinforce despotism yet also act as a consultative check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communism undermines industry without coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C113: Montesquieu argues (editor concurs) that where the prince or entire people is sole proprietor, industry and agriculture decline because people rely on the state; such regime depends on forced labor and yields stagnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use economic incentives and property rights as criteria for productive societies; collectivization risks slavery-like coercion and stunting civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotic succession by selection is ultimate despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C115: 'Choisir son successeur.' — the ability of the prince to choose his successor exemplifies extreme despotism; heredity acts as a check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutionalize succession rules (heredity, laws) to limit arbitrary concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit honors and decorations to avoid corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C123: Distinctions purely honorary and without money are compatible with republics, but excessive number/extension of decorations is a sign of corruption; limiting decorations is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain restraint in honorary rewards to preserve their symbolic value and avoid patronage corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proportionate punishment and protect against cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Note C130: Voltaire critiques Montesquieu's example of death for a sparrow as disproportionate; nevertheless protecting animals from cruelty can prevent cruelty to humans (cites law Grammont).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penal policy should be proportionate; legislating against animal cruelty can be justified as part of moral legal order.
